SEC14A-01.note: Inverted sentence: subject is 'two silver pennies' (plural), far after the verb; narrative past (1911, 'forced'). A 'was tucked' is strongest, attracted by 'slab'/'parchment'. Options form a clean 2x2 (number x tense) so nothing falls free.

SEC14A-02.note: Head noun 'practice' (singular) separated by a long relative clause ending in plural 'sources'; sentence needs a finite verb, so A/B leave a fragment. C 'have given' is the attractor-driven distractor and strongest.

SEC14A-03.note: Colon introduces the list anticipated by 'four separate pieces of information'. B semicolon fails: what follows is a noun-phrase list, not a clause. C makes a fragment. D 'which the direction...' is garbled and drops on sight.

SEC14A-04.note: Correlative 'so high a multiple ... that [result clause]' takes no punctuation before 'that'. The 'so' is far back, so A 'mine, that' is strongest; D 'so that' duplicates 'so'; B colon breaks the correlative. Garden path: 'mine that' first reads as a relative clause.

SEC14A-05.note: 'Whatever he wrote ... has seldom survived' is its own independent clause (free-relative subject), so a sentence break is needed. A comma splice is strongest because 'whatever' reads like a trailing modifier; B is a run-on; C 'that whatever' is garbled and drops free.

SEC14A-06.note: 'boards ... facing' has no finite verb, so it works only as the object of the participle 'leaving'. A, C and D each turn 'the boards ... facing' into a clause with no verb (a fragment or a broken subordinate clause). C/D are plausible connectives.

SEC14B-01.note: Subject is the noun clause 'Whether those spores survive...' (singular). 'since the first feeding trials of the 1980s' requires the present perfect. A 'have kept' (attracted by 'truffles'/'squirrels') is strongest. 2x2 grid of number x aspect, so nothing drops free.

SEC14B-02.note: Relative pronoun is the object of 'considered' -> whom. The judgment ended in 1998 ('until a 1998 expedition found'), so simple past, not present perfect. Who/whom case is not on the DSAT Form/Structure/Sense list; the tense half is. D (who + past) is strongest.
SEC14B-02.drop_reason: Off blueprint: the case half (who/whom) is not on the digital SAT Form, Structure, and Sense list, and it decides 2 of the 3 distractors (B, D). Key and explanation are correct. Fix: re-author it as a pure tense or agreement item.

SEC14B-03.note: Dangling modifier: 'Bleached nearly white...' must attach to the lichen, so the lichen must be the main-clause subject. A 'the lichen's first collector' is the strong possessive trap (subject is 'collector'); B and C plainly put a person first.

SEC14B-04.note: Two independent clauses: semicolon, with 'after sunset' introducing the second. A is a comma splice; C attaches 'after sunset' to the wrong clause and is still a splice; D 'which the concentration...' is garbled and drops free.

SEC14B-05.note: Introductory subordinate clause 'While ... cools' followed by a comma, then the main clause 'a seed crystal ... grows'. B misreads 'cools' as transitive (garden path) and leaves no subject for 'grows'; C makes the 'While' clause a fragment; D puts 'and' after a subordinate clause.

SEC14B-06.note: The appositive 'a cyanobacterium whose cells measure ... and slip ...' needs a relative 'whose' so it stays a modifier, closed before 'accounts'. D is a comma splice inside the appositive (strongest). A and B split the subject from 'accounts' and drop almost at sight.

tells: Lone-mark-is-key: in the boundary items the key is the only option with its mark: 03 (only colon), 05 (only period), B04 (only semicolon). It does not decide 04, 06, B05 or B06, where commas repeat or the key has no mark, but it decides three of the six boundary items outright.

Added connective/relative is never the key in 03 (D 'which'), 04 (D 'so that'), 05 (C 'that'), 06 (C 'although', D 'whereupon'), B04 (D 'which'), B05 (C 'Then', D 'and'). B06 breaks it (key adds 'whose'), so it is a strong but not perfect elimination heuristic: it strikes one or two distractors per item.
The 'X, which the ...' garbled distractor recurs verbatim in shape (03 D, B04 D) and always loses on sight.

Form items 01 and B01 use the identical 2x2 option grid (singular/plural x two tenses/aspects); in both the key is the plural/singular cell opposite the attractor noun next to the blank. A 'pick the number opposite the nearest noun' heuristic decides 01, 02 and B01.
near_duplicates: SEC14A-01 / SEC14B-01: same 2x2 number-by-tense verb grid, with a distant true subject and an adjacent noun attractor.
SEC14A-02 / SEC14B-01: long subject (head noun or noun clause) with a plural attractor ending right at the blank.
SEC14A-03 / SEC14B-04: same option template (mark A / mark B / mark C / ', which the'), with the key being the lone mark.
SEC14A-05 / SEC14B-04: comma-splice boundary with the key as the lone strong mark (period / semicolon).

phase2_note: All 12 keys match grader d's cold answers. Every explanation's reasoning holds for the key and each distractor. Batch-level and not a per-item drop: the lone-strong-mark key on A-05 (period among commas) and B-04 (semicolon among commas) remains a cross-item tell. In A-03 every option carries a different mark, so it is not a lone-mark tell there.
